title: The Spec Is the Interface
description: Nine tools that put requirements, decisions and approvals back in front of the agent, from reviewed specs and sliceable standards to PHP agent runtimes.
content:
# The Spec Is the Interface

The failure mode of agent-written software is not that the code is wrong. It is that the code is right about the wrong thing, and nobody notices until a rule that lived in a closed ticket gets quietly broken.

The tools in this piece all attack that from a different angle, but they share one belief: the artifact you hand an agent matters more than the prompt you write. A ticket describes a change. A spec describes the product.

## Write the decision down

[[link:/tools/2212|SpecDeck]] makes the case with a concrete example: your shop takes discount codes, you ask an agent to give members 10 percent off, and it builds exactly that — except the decision that discounts never stack was in a ticket the agent never saw. SpecDeck keeps project context, requirements and acceptance criteria in one reviewed spec, works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and OpenClaw, and ships an AI assistant so product colleagues can join the review.

[[link:/tools/2225|SLCR]] turns the same idea into an open standard: sliceable, linked, checkable requirements. Each requirement can be handed to an agent alone, with the context it links to and nothing else, so the rest of the spec stays out of the context window. Requirements combine with AND, OR and XOR, acceptance criteria map to validators you already run, and slcr check reports what is met in CI.

[[link:/tools/2223|Enso Method]] is the discipline rather than the format. It is an open-source set of over 20 agent skills for Claude Code and Codex: requirements settled up front, open questions answered or recorded as assumptions, and every acceptance criterion proven before the work is called done. Its own framing is the sharpest line in this group — the fix is not a better prompt, it is doing the thinking before the build.

[[link:/tools/2224|Toolmaker Agent]] takes the collaborative route. Humans and coding agents share one structured record of what you build, shipped as a single binary that runs locally, with documentation published as plain text for agents to read.

[[link:/tools/2232|Arketum]] adds the gate. It is an MCP server with one build tool that the agent calls at every step; each answer says where the work stands and what comes next, and the person confirms what will be done before it is built. It runs nothing and calls no model, which keeps it cheap, and it is candid about the limit: it can verify that a decision was respected, not that the decision was good.

## Skills as the unit

If the spec is what to build, a skill is how. [[link:/tools/2216|SkillWire]] is a searchable catalog that also runs a paired trial before you trust one: it pins the source, shows every warning line it matched, downloads a ZIP with original bytes and file hashes, then freezes your task and grader so both arms start from the same files and you review the artifacts blind.

## Standards for what agents build

[[link:/tools/2240|Open Components]] is a written standard for UI components across three axes, and the third is the new one. User experience and developer experience are familiar; agentic experience is not. It asks for semantic roles agents can read from markup, anatomy and props published as machine-readable specs, deterministic rendering, and rules an agent can check its own work against before shipping.

## Orchestration and runtime

[[link:/tools/2243|RondoFlow]] is a local-first, MIT-licensed platform for visually orchestrating Claude Code agents: drag agents onto a canvas, attach skills, define security policy per agent and run the workflow on your own machine with your own files. It is early, at 26 stars, but it is the first readable answer to what multi-agent orchestration should look like outside a YAML file.

[[link:/tools/2244|phpClaw]] is for the other half of the web. It is an open-source AI agent framework for PHP with tools, memory, security guards and a ReAct loop already built, zero framework dependencies in core, adapters for Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Joomla, OpenCart and PrestaShop, and any LLM provider through an environment variable.

## The security case

[[link:/tools/2234|Casco]] is the reminder that all of this ships to production. It is an AI-native application security platform built on continuous pentesting: agents sign in as real users with their own identity, email, phone and TOTP device, test authenticated workflows behind Cloudflare and CAPTCHAs, prove exploitable paths with reproducible evidence and retest the fix. It also publishes a free CVE feed for agents, which is the smallest and most useful piece of the product.

## The pattern

Five of these nine tools are about writing something down before code exists. That is not a coincidence and it is not nostalgia for waterfall. It is the observation that an agent's context window is a budget, and a prose spec spends it badly while a structured requirement spends it well.

[[link:/tools/2225|SLCR]] makes the requirement a first-class artifact. [[link:/tools/2232|Arketum]] makes the approval a recorded event. [[link:/tools/2212|SpecDeck]] makes the review a shared surface. And [[link:/tools/2240|Open Components]] extends the same rigour to the output, which is where most teams discover the problem too late.

Pick one and the rest of the group becomes optional. Pick none and you are back to hoping the guess was good.
tldr: Agents guess whenever you leave a gap. SpecDeck, SLCR, Enso Method, Toolmaker Agent and Arketum all move the thinking before the build, while SkillWire, Open Components, RondoFlow, phpClaw and Casco cover skills, UI standards, orchestration, runtime and security.
